title: Fostering Digital Citizenship: Proactive Strategies for Student Well-being ent-well-being-fc482f50d740
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek writes to school leaders about the harm engagement-driven social media does to students, starting from his own experience of agitation and his decision to leave Facebook. He argues that before schools move students into online discussion they should teach plain interpersonal skills, such as responding with care, building on ideas and respecting disagreement. He offers concrete moves: silent discussion stations, student-written online norms, student-led digital citizenship campaigns and a mandatory digital driver's ed course. He then frames digital wellness as a leadership duty, to be handled through prevention, media literacy and modeling positive school social media use instead of discipline after cyberbullying occurs. The piece sits in the school-policy side of ed-tech, consistent with the author's other archived work.
points: Teach offline communication skills before students enter online discussion, because those skills transfer directly to digital platforms.
Silent discussion stations give students a low-stakes way to practice constructive written dialogue and then draft their own online norms.
A mandatory 'digital driver's ed' course before independent social media use would signal that the school takes responsible digital navigation seriously.
Prevention beats punishment: school-wide empathy programs and tech breaks head off cyberbullying instead of reacting to it.
Leaders model the standard by using school accounts to highlight achievement and kindness rather than only logistics.
quotes: While digital literacy remains an important educational goal, a shift in priorities is needed. Before transitioning students to online discussions, consider emphasizing fundamental, readily transferable interpersonal communication skills. Tactics like carefully considered responses, building upon ideas rather than negation, and respecting differing viewpoints lay the groundwork for healthy digital interactions.

I know what it’s like to see students sucked into endless social media cycles. The arguments and posturing become like magnets, pulling students away from in-person conversations and into divisive online battles.

Silent Discussion Stations: Arrange pods equipped with large paper, markers, and a central discussion prompt. Students silently build conversational threads in writing, prioritizing constructive contributions.

Instead of solely punishing cyberbullying incidents as they occur, implement school-wide programs addressing empathy, respect in online settings, and healthy “tech breaks.” This preventative approach builds awareness and skills at a broader level, creating a proactive, less reactive environment where negative situations are less likely to even begin.

Media literacy curriculum teaches students to critically evaluate online content, empowering them to identify misinformation, resist impulsive clicks on inflammatory headlines, and recognize when social media use starts feeling unhealthily addictive. This strengthens their ability to maintain focus on schoolwork and builds internal coping mechanisms against the constant onslaught of online stimulation.

Our role as school leaders extends far beyond test scores and graduation rates. We shape the whole student, building strong citizens for the modern world. With social media platforms too often amplifying conflict and anxiety, how can we proactively promote digital well-being? Focusing on healthy practices becomes part of our accountability for academic excellence and resilient students prepared for the world they’ll live in.
